old: I leaned my forehead against it, and they helped me, and I lifted it at last

old: You leaned on him the way a man leans on his wife, and he will never leave you.
new: You loved him the way a man loves his wife, and held him close, and he will never leave you.
why: SB I: Ninsun's reading repeats the dream's 'you loved it like a wife, caressed and embraced it'; matches the restored line in seg-0014. unverified against a bundled source.

old: and the open ground of Ishtar's temple — three square miles and a half
new: and half a square mile for Ishtar's temple — three square miles and a half
why: SB I 22-23: one sar city, one sar date grove, one sar clay pit, half a sar Ishtar's temple, three and a half sar is Uruk. Without the half the sum does not add up. Same fix in XI seg-0019. unverified against a bundled source.

old: hard as the war-god himself

old: You have grown wise, Enkidu. You have become like a god.
new: You are handsome, Enkidu. You are like a god.
why: SB I 207 damqāta Enkidu: 'you are handsome / fine', not 'wise'; his widened understanding is already in the narration just before. unverified against a bundled source.

old: So he read his dreams.
new: So Gilgamesh told his dreams.
why: Ninsun reads the dreams; Gilgamesh tells them. The tablet closes on the dreams being told; 'read' points at the wrong person.

old: There is no shame in this. You are what they say you are.
why: Enkidu's speech ends with Enlil granting Gilgamesh the kingship; the two closing sentences are added commentary on how to take the fight (work-wide policy: commentary is cut). unverified against a bundled source.

old: beasts. Now there will never be quiet in Uruk again.” And the men were glad, in spite of themselves:

old: the bed was laid for the goddess and the bride;
new: the bed was laid for the goddess Ishhara;
why: SB II: 'for Ishhara the bed was laid'. Proper-noun policy: restore the name where one phrase does it. unverified against a bundled source.

old: — the friend who saves his friend, the companion who will never let the other stand alone.
why: Not in this passage; an echo of Ninsun's words in Tablet I added as commentary (work-wide policy).

old: There is a crying in my throat and nothing to fight. My arms have gone slack. The life is draining out of me from doing nothing.

old: What hard road has you out at this pace?
new: What hard road are you on?

old: She did not weep where they could see her, for she was a goddess and the mother of the king; but her heart had said what a mother's heart says.

old: After this much is lost — some lines broken away from the clay, so that we cannot follow every word. When the tablet can be read again, the heroes are making their last preparations, and Gilgamesh is leaving word for the keeping of Uruk while he is gone.

old: — and here the tablet breaks off, with the gate of the city behind them and the mountain still far ahead.

old: [A long stretch of Tablet III is missing — perhaps sixty lines, and the closing lines as well. What survives of the departure, and the road itself, is taken up in Tablet IV.]

old: and every storm wind there is. Set them on him so that Gilgamesh and Enkidu can stand against his face. Let the winds be the weapons of my son.”

old: There were more dreams along the road, and not all of them can be read now, for the clay is broken. old: They saw the cedar mountain, the home of the gods, the throne of Irnini. From the face of the mountain the cedars threw down their shade, and the shade was rich and full of rest, and the path that ran up into the wood was thick with brush, and it was good to walk.

old: Beside the two of us we were no bigger than reeds in a marsh.

old: And Enkidu, who was born in the wild and knew the meaning of such things, said to him:

old: For this was the garden Humbaba walked in, and the noise of it was his pleasure, and he listened to it the way a king listens to musicians at his table.

old: May the two of you never grow old together. May Enkidu have no portion of life beyond his friend Gilgamesh — let him not outlive this day's work.

old: I dreamed it in the night.” And this was the dream he told. Anu and Enlil and Ea, and Shamash of the bright sky, sat down together to judge. Because the two of us killed Humbaba, and because we struck down the Bull of Heaven, one of us must die. So the gods had decided, and now they were deciding which. Enlil said, “Let Enkidu die. Gilgamesh shall not die.” Then Shamash spoke up for Enkidu: “Was it not at my word that they killed the Bull of Heaven and killed Humbaba? Shall innocent Enkidu die for that?” But Enlil turned on him in anger: “You went down with them, day after day, as if you were one of their company. That is why you speak for them.” And the council held, and the doom stood, and the dream broke off there.
new: I dreamed it in the night. Anu and Enlil and Ea, and Shamash of the bright sky, sat down together to judge. Because the two of us killed Humbaba, and because we struck down the Bull of Heaven, one of us must die. So the gods had decided, and now they were deciding which. Enlil said, ‘Let Enkidu die. Gilgamesh shall not die.’ Then Shamash spoke up for me: ‘Was it not at my word that they killed the Bull of Heaven and killed Humbaba? Shall innocent Enkidu die for that?’ But Enlil turned on him in anger: ‘You went down with them, day after day, as if you were one of their company. That is why you speak for them.’ And the council held, and the doom stood, and then I woke.”
why: The dream starts in third person and slides into Enkidu's 'the two of us' with no quotation mark. Kept wholly inside Enkidu's speech, as in the Hittite prose summary that supplies this opening; inner speeches take single quotes; wording otherwise unchanged except 'spoke up for me' and 'then I woke'. unverified against a bundled source.

old: ; let you be honored, and let you be the mother of a great household.”

old: For the dead must be welcomed below, and a man goes better among them when the gods who keep that country have been given their honor. old: Only fragments survive on the clay: a flask, a throwing-stick of fine wood, vessels of carnelian and lapis, weapons and ornaments, each presented to a named netherworld power so that Enkidu will be received and well treated below. The full list cannot be recovered, and Lectio does not invent it; the broken clay is left broken.]
new: Parts of it survive: a flask, a throwing-stick of fine wood, vessels of carnelian and lapis, weapons and ornaments, each presented to a named netherworld power. The full list cannot be read.]

old: [The close of Tablet VIII — the last of the funeral rites and Gilgamesh's leaving of the city — is lost in the break, and is taken up at the head of Tablet IX, where Gilgamesh is already roaming the open country, grieving for Enkidu and afraid, for the first time, of his own death.]

old: All the while one thought worked in him and would not let him go. Enkidu had died, and the body of his friend had gone back to clay. So Gilgamesh thought of Uta-napishti — Uta-napishti the Distant, the one man who had lived through the Flood and not died, whom the gods had taken up and given life that has no end. If any living being knew how a man escapes death, it was he. “I will go to Uta-napishti,” Gilgamesh said. “I will go to him, far off as he is, and ask him how he found the everlasting life, and how I may have it too.” And he
new: And he
why: Narrator's reasoning in place of the source's resolve, which now stands in seg-0001; 'gone back to clay' is borrowed from Tablet X. The segment keeps its last sentence. unverified against a bundled source.

old: [Here a stretch of the tablet is broken away — some two dozen lines — and we lose the words of his roaming and his grief before the text can be read again.]

old: At three double-hours the dark was thick, and there was no light: he could see nothing before him and nothing behind. At four double-hours the dark was thick, and there was no light: nothing before, nothing behind. He kept on going. At five double-hours the dark was thick, and there was no light, and it let him see neither ahead nor behind. At six double-hours the dark was thick, the same thick dark, and he went on through it.

At four double-hours the dark was thick, and there was no light: it would not let him see ahead or behind. He kept on going. At five double-hours the dark was thick, and there was no light: it would not let him see ahead or behind. At six double-hours the dark was thick, and there was no light: it would not let him see ahead or behind. He kept on going.
why: SB IX repeats the formula word for word; the variations weaken the litany. Only the formula changes. unverified against a bundled source.

old: it would not let him see what lay before him or behind him.

old: This is the wall he came home to, the one thing that would stand. He had gone to the ends of the earth and come back with empty hands; the plant was gone, and the secret of the gods was a secret still, and a man must die. But the city would not die. The brick he had fired, the wall he had raised — that was the life that would outlast him, the only kind a man is given to keep. And so the story ends where it began, on the wall of Uruk, looking down at the work of his hands.
why: SB XI ends on Gilgamesh's words about the wall, repeating the prologue. Everything after them is the editor's moral written in as the epic's last lines. The segment keeps the journey home and the speech. unverified against a bundled source.

old: "So she baked the loaves and set them by his head, and she marked the wall for each day he slept. The first loaf had gone hard as a stone. The second was like leather. The third was soggy. And the seventh — he was still asleep when Uta-napishti reached out and touched him, and Gilgamesh woke. Your first loaf is a stone; your second is leather; the third is soggy; the fourth has gone white; the fifth is gray with mold; the sixth is still fresh — and the seventh, you were sleeping when I touched you.' And Gilgamesh said: 'Uta-napishti, what am I to do now? Where am I to go? A thief has taken hold of my body. Death is sitting in my bedroom, and wherever I set my foot, there death is.'

The crust of the fourth had turned white. The fifth was gray with mold. The sixth was still fresh. And the seventh — he was still asleep when Uta-napishti reached out and touched him, and Gilgamesh woke. And Gilgamesh said to him: "Sleep had hardly poured over me, and you reached out and touched me and woke me!" But Uta-napishti said: "Look at the loaves, Gilgamesh. Count them. Your first loaf is a stone; your second is leather; the third is soggy; the fourth has gone white; the fifth is gray with mold; the sixth is still fresh — and the seventh, you were sleeping when I touched you." And Gilgamesh said: "Uta-napishti, what am I to do now? Where am I to go? A thief has taken hold of my body. Death is sitting in my bedroom, and wherever I set my foot, there death is."
why: Uta-napishti's tale ends in seg-0014; this segment is narration but opened with a double quotation mark, so the speech inside dropped to single quotes. Opening mark removed and inner speech given double quotes, matching seg-0014 and seg-0016 (straight here; the quote policy curls them with the rest of X-XI).
